old:
Everything above starts the dial in 205 BC, because three published studies put its first full moon on 12 May of that year. I wanted to see how firm that is.

I tried every month from 300 BC to 1 BC as the dial's first, 3,711 of them. Sixteen, counting 205 BC itself, fit the dial's marked months at least as well as 205 BC does. So the marks cannot date the dial by themselves, which is what one of the three studies, by Carman and Evans, had already said.

What decides among the sixteen is a detail not yet mentioned: beside each mark the dial gives an hour of the day or of the night. Set against the real times of full and new moon, the hours fit four of the sixteen, the starts of 223, 205, 187 and 169 BC, which are one eighteen-year cycle apart. The cycle is about a third of a day longer than a whole number of days, so each of the four fits at a place about a third of the way round the world from the one before. Taking the hours as they are engraved, 205 BC is the only one of the four that puts the dial in the Greek world, at about the longitude of the Aegean Sea.

That is the argument Carman and Evans published in 2014. I worked it again with programs of my own and came to the same year.

why: OPTIONAL, and INSTEAD OF readable.json why-1 and why-2 (it covers the same text). The whole section in one paragraph, for an author who wants the story shorter. What it leaves out is already under the fold in 'The hours': the 3,711 months, the four starts the hours fit, the places a third of the world apart, and the longitude of the Aegean. It makes no statement the four paragraphs do not make; it only stops sooner.
